title: Certifying Karp–Rabin fingerprints
formal: For every fixed integer \(c\ge2\), is there a uniform randomized algorithm that, given a string \(T\in\{0,\ldots,\sigma-1\}^n\), with \(n\ge2\), \(2\le\sigma\le n^c\), and a supplied prime \(p\le n^c\), certifies in \(O(n\log n)\) worst-case time whether the Karp–Rabin fingerprint modulo \(p\) is collision-free on all equal-length substrings of \(T\)? No input having a collision may ever be certified; every collision-free input must be certified with probability at least \(2/3\).
definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. The input symbols and prime are given as integers; primality is promised. Use \(w=\lceil(4c+10)\log_2(n+2)\rceil\)-bit words, so a constant number of words suffices for all modular products. For length \(\ell\ge1\) and start \(0\le i\le n-\ell\), define \(h_p(T[i..i+\ell-1])=\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}T[i+j]\sigma^j\bmod p\). A collision is a triple \((i,j,\ell)\) of valid starts and a length for which the two strings differ but their fingerprints are equal. Equal strings with equal fingerprints are not collisions; fingerprints of different lengths need not be separated. The algorithm returns CERTIFIED or REJECT. The probability is over its internal random bits for each fixed \((T,\sigma,p)\); false rejection is permitted only with probability at most \(1/3\) on collision-free inputs. The given prime and base must be preserved. All preprocessing counts toward time, space is at most the number of words writable in that time, and there is no externally supplied suffix index or precomputed table.
why: Efficient certification could turn a widely used probabilistic string primitive into a reliable one while preserving a chosen fingerprint representation.

context_blocks.text: Farach-Colton asks whether all substring lengths can be checked in linear time or at least in n log n time for a supplied string and prime. A quadratic-time method is straightforward using suffix trees.

The source allows rejecting a collision-free fingerprint with small probability. This formulation makes the one-sided error direction explicit and selects the n log n target; the stricter linear-time question remains context.

sentences: A string and a prime modulus are supplied as input.
Each substring has a polynomial fingerprint using the supplied modulus.
The question asks whether any unequal substrings of the same length collide.
The target is n log n time with no false certification of a bad modulus.
A collision-free modulus may be rejected with bounded probability.
